new_statements.quote: There are two contrastive tones in Defaka: high and low. There are also two contour tones HL LH which arise from the combination of the two contrastive tones on a monosyllabic word containing a long vowel or diphthong. Finally, Bob-Manuel (1990) reports a downstepped high tone ꜜH resulting from a HLH sequence of tones. [...] Finally, there are two tones in Defaka which give rise to five distinct tonal patterns: H, L, HL, LH, and HꜜH. The L, HL, and HꜜH tonal contrasts are similar in that they are realized phonetically as a falling F0 contour.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Defaka is a two-tone language (H, L) with downstep; tone, not stress, is the lexical prosodic contrast. The only instrumental/phonological description says nothing about word stress or accent at all, so no stress placement rule can be stated. Akinlabi & Connell (WOCAL 6, 2009, p. 1, 11) add that Defaka 'remains a true tone system' and has 'resisted the gradual movement in the direction of an accentual system which is now widespread in Ijoid'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. On tone: the F0 study found the falling patterns L, HL and HꜜH not significantly distinct at onset, middle or offset (p. 16), which the authors say 'may draw into question the phonological status' of e.g. the HL vs HꜜH contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on isolated citation forms (wordlist elicitation, 12 male speakers recorded Aug. 1994 at Univ. of Port Harcourt and in Nkoroo). Sentence-level pitch (question marking by heightened pitch / suspended declination) is treated only in Connell et al. 2009 ACAL 40 slides.
new_statements.identity_note: Shryock et al. (p. 3) describe the Defaka of the Defaka ward of Nkoroo town; they caution that 'the phonetics and phonology of the language we are describing are heavily influenced by the Nkoroo dialect of Ijo [nkor1239], and the two languages may be indistinguishable at this level' (both principal informants from mixed Defaka-Nkoroo marriages). Akinlabi & Connell 2009 argue against this: the Defaka tone system stays distinct from Nkoroo, which is drifting toward an accentual system.
